MR. PITMAN-ALLEGED ABUSE OF POWER BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects every member in this house. My question of privilege is this. The Minister of Agriculture has grossly violated the rights of parliament and assumed powers beyond those authorized for him by substituting the powers of his department for the legislative powers of this parliament.
If I may direct your attention to the order paper for today you will see item No. 4, which reads "Second reading of Bill C-77, an act to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada." Yesterday there came to my office not one, not two but 50 copies of a pamphlet which announces the agricultural rehabilitation and development act. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no agricultural rehabilitation and development act on the statute books of this nation. This pamphlet was produced by the information division of the Department of Agriculture, and some of us will remember some of the pungent comments that were made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on that particular branch when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were being considered.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a flagrant abuse of the powers of this department. I suggest to you that this pamphlet states how A.R.D.A. will operate. How can the people of Canada be told how A.R.D.A. will operate when this bill has not received second reading? Is there a suggestion that second reading has no effect? Is it the contention that a debate in this house amounts to nothing more than the rubber-stamping of a measure?

BUTTER AND CHEESE
subsubtopic: OP SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has authorized the agricultural stabilization board to continue the present level of price support for the dairy industry for the period May 1, 1961, to April 30, 1962.
There are two dairy products presently under price support. Price support for butter is 64 cents per pound for Canada first grade creamery butter scoring 40-93, basis delivery Montreal, with appropriate price differentials for other grades and qualities. Ontario cheese, Canada first grade waxed, f.o.b. warehouse, is presently supported at

32 cents per pound; and Quebec cheese, Canada first grade waxed, basis delivery Montreal, is supported at 31J cents per pound.
The price support for these two dairy commodities for the 12-month period May 1, 1961, to April 30, 1962, will continue at these levels. In addition, 25 cents per hundred pounds will continue to be paid for whole milk delivered for manufacturing purposes, exclusive of milk from producers who sell a portion of their milk in the fluid bottled milk market.
The stabilization board will continue for the present to support the price of butter and cheese by purchasing these products from suppliers at the prescribed support levels. Should any change be made subsequently in the method of support, an announcement will be made well in advance to give the industry sufficient time to make any necessary adjustments. Regardless of the method of support used, however, the level of support to producers now authorized will continue during the 12-month period from May 1, 1961, to April 30, 1962.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the light of all the propaganda that is being directed across the country against price support programs for the dairy industry, I am pleased that the government has announced the continuation of support prices on these dairy products. I always give the government credit when credit is due.
The announcement will reassure the dairy industry, particularly as the minister has assured dairy producers that the government will continue to purchase their products at these fixed support prices. This means a real guarantee and is in no way a phony guarantee such as would come from an average price deficiency support program. The minister has left the door open to a change in method, but he did seem to assure the dairy industry that even if the method is changed these particular guarantees to the producers will be maintained. Apparently for the coming year the dairy industry will have the support prices continued that they have enjoyed to date.
The minister left unanswered the question whether consumers will be allowed to purchase butter at lower prices in order

to move it onto the markets. Perhaps the minister will have an announcement on this matter at a later time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. The man in question, Griffin, served in the Canadian navy for some time, from which he was released because of a pulhems S-5 rating. Subsequently he enlisted in the Canadian army under his brother's name and served in the army from January, 1957 to July, 1957. His proper name finally became known and he was released, again with an S-5 pulhems profile.
With regard to the statement which I am told he made on television last night that Canadian .303 rifles, Bren guns and Sten guns stolen from Camp Gagetown were issued to these people alleged to have been recruited in Canada, I am informed there have never been any .303 rifles, Bren guns or Sten guns issued at Camp Gagetown. From the time the camp opened the new rifle was issued there. There have been no thefts at Camp Gagetown since January 1 of 1960, except for one pistol.

Therefore the allegation that these were Canadian rifles, Bren guns and Sten guns stolen from Camp Gagetown is completely incorrect.

Mr. Chairman, it is really an impertinence to get up a second time on the first item of the minister's estimates, but I think I have a point that will interest the committee and I am sure will interest the minister. The Liberal party established a provisional kind of shadow cabinet to sit opposite the government departments in order to keep check. We all know the flair, the elan, and the wit which the hon. member for St. Denis has applied to this task. He has taken it with a great deal of seriousness. In a sense he has met the minister on many points of conflict, and we have had a great deal of humour and wit in the house with regard to the Post Office Department.
This is in a tradition. When the Conservatives were in the opposition the present Postmaster General was very much to the fore as the critic of the post office in that particular party grouping. We know how, with perhaps not quite the wit or the elan but certainly with even more persistence and study, he continually analysed and criticized the Post Office Department. Just the other day the Postmaster General was taken very much to task for the fact that he had failed to really carry out all the changes and improvements he had advocated when he was in this shadow cabinet position.
I hope that my remarks when I first spoke on this item indicated that I at least as an individual member have a great respect for the way in which the minister has gone into the operations of his department. Whatever the criticisms we may make, I think he has made an inordinate effort in relation to the job, more than most ministers do, in order to master all the details of the department. In fact he has become so knowledgeable about

all details that it is really superfluous for him to have in front of him the officials of the department. We have here a minister who really knows all the aspects of his department's operations and who is prepared to give them at the drop of the hat.
Being aware of this situation, being somewhat of a suspicious mind-I hope not in a bad sense-and having a few pipe lines, and by that I mean avenues of communication- to various parts of Ottawa, a couple of things have struck me in relation to this department. As I say, the minister is much more knowledgeable than the average minister about the operations of his department. Normally the estimates of the Post Office Department come in later in the year. This tends to be the pattern. I found out-and I could be corrected in this respect-that the deputy minister of this particular department, the civil servant in charge, seems to be due for retirement in May, 1961. These two pieces of information I began to put together with a little bit of questioning and a little bit of probing. I have a very hot tip, you might say, for the committee and it is to the effect that we may be able to look forward to having this extremely competent and knowledgeable minister of the crown as the next deputy minister in charge of the Post Office Department.
That knocks you out.

I am afraid I have not the knowledge of the Post Office Department which is possessed by the Postmaster General. It seems to me that this suggestion opens up all kinds of prospects. At by-elections the question will be asked whether it is a case of little furry animals deserting the ship and all that sort of thing. I hate to put it from that point of view, but I raise the spectre for the committee. Suppose-and I am not conceding it for a moment-that at the next election the Liberal party should win.
They will win.
Suppose they pick their shadow cabinet critic, the hon. member for St. Denis to become Postmaster General. I ask you to conceive of this situation.
Oh, oh.

I ask you to conceive of the hon. member for St. Denis as Postmaster General and the present minister as deputy postmaster general. This leads me to present to the minister several questions. I should like to know whether it is true that we are to have at some time in the near future a replacement, because of retirement or other circumstances of the deputy minister in charge of the department. I should also like him to tell me whether this mastery he has gained

of the department is again going to be put to such use as I have indicated or, in other words, whether we can look forward to his being a senior civil servant.
I have not any criticism to present of this particular trend. I know there is some criticism of the other government to the effect that they used to take people out of the civil service and put them into the cabinet. I do not think it is such a bad thing.

I always listen with
interest to the hon. member. I have followed his remarks today, but up to the present time I have been unable to ascertain whether he is making a political speech or telling us a fairy tale. May we know which it is?
It is the same thing.

I cannot tell the hon. member whether it is a fairy tale. As a private member the hon. member knows how difficult it is for a private member to confirm all these things. However, I was trying to put together a few points that have come to my attention and, quite frankly, a rather hot tip. I thought this was the place, namely on the minister's estimates just before he makes a statement, to ask him whether he could enlighten us upon this possibility. As I say, I am not being political. I would not mind seeing the Postmaster General as the senior civil servant of the department. I do not know what are the views of other hon. members, but I am willing to admit that he is extremely knowledgeable about this department. However, there is raised, as I said, the issue of the hon. member for St. Denis vis-a-vis the deputy minister. It also raises the question of instead of elevating civil servants to the cabinet, making members of the cabinet civil servants. I believe this to a degree is a new trend, and I think we would welcome the minister's comments upon this particular point of view.

think perhaps at this time I should deal with some of the points raised in the last day and a half, and perhaps first and immediately with the fantasy which the hon. member for Port Arthur has built upon the one and only piece of information that is known or even under consideration, as far as I know, by anyone. I refer to the fact that the deputy minister reaches the normal age of retirement some time during this summer. The appointment of deputy ministers rests with the Prime Minister. Certainly if the hon. member calls that a hot tip, I call it rather cold information.

In view of the fact that the hon. member for Port Arthur has announced that he does not intend to run for parliament again, would the minister consider the appointment of the present hon. member for Port Arthur as the suocessor to the present deputy minister in the Post Office Department?

The
only thing I have to say on that matter is that undoubtedly if it were done he would be much happier under me than under the other supposition that the hon. member for St. Denis would be postmaster general.
Having as definitely as I can dispelled any of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Port Arthur with regard to the deputy postmaster general, I want to thank him very much indeed for the compliment. The long experience and background of the present deputy and the contribution he has made to the department over the years mean that his shoes are going to be big and difficult ones to fit. Anyone who is even considered for the post should certainly be proud.
Listening to the comments of the various opposition members and the criticisms of the department I could not help but remember a story. I think this perhaps sums up their attitude as I see it. This is the story of the guide who had a rather remarkable hunting dog of which he was very proud. The guide took a member of the opposition out duck hunting. They got into the blind, and after they had been there a little while the ducks started going in. They shot one of the ducks and it fell into the water. The guide turned to his remarkable dog and said "Fetch". The dog started off after the duck, and the remarkable thing about the dog was that, having large paws, he ran across the water rather than swimming to pick up the duck.
He picked up the duck and brought it back into the blind. The member of the opposition said absolutely nothing about this. The guide was rather upset that nothing had been said, and he turned to the member of the opposition and said, "Didn't you notice anything remarkable about the dog?" The member of the opposition said, "Yes; he can't swim".
It seems to me it is possible for the opposition to overlook all the accomplishments of all the different groups in the department and at the same time pick away, without foundation in most cases, at a few things which some hon. members suggest imply that there is something wrong. As far as I am concerned the criticism that has been levelled against me by hon. member after hon. member, of taking too much pride in the Post Office Department and its accomplishments and reporting them with too much pride to this house-to the extent that this criticism

is made and is true, I am very happy. I am immensely proud of what this department and every person in it has accomplished. I have no apology to make for the way in which my statement was presented on behalf of the department.
I want to thank all hon. members who have participated in the debate. Their helpful ideas will be given every consideration. I will reply now to as many of the points as possible. Others can be raised on the individual items, or where we have not the information available now we will answer by correspondence as rapidly as possible.
I want to say to the hon. member for St. Denis that I regret the general attitude he took, that this debate is a time for buffoonery. The House of Commons has ample opportunity, and sometimes ample need, for humour. Certainly we appreciate it, but the House of Commons is not a burlesque house, as I felt some of his remarks tended to make it. The report of his speech made news right across the country. However, it was not the type of news which I think in general helped the reputation of this house as a chamber of serious debate. The height of his contribution -if one can dignify any particular item by having any height, though I suppose that among mole hills almost anything is a mountain-was the question of automation, mechanization and postal progress.
I gather that the hon. member is against such measures, although it is a little hard to tell. He is reported in Hansard as saying, and I use his exact words:
(Translation):
I am all for progress, but I am against it-
(Text):
The English translation of these remarks is officially:
I am all for progress, but I am against it.
Again on the same item, as reported at page 3640 of Hansard, the hon. member said: (Translation):
I am all In favour of forging ahead and keeping in step with other countries, but... I think it is time to put a stop to such experiments-
(Text):
The official English translation is:
I am all in favour of forging ahead and keeping in step with other countries, but... I think it is time to put a stop to such experiments ...
I do not think we have ever heard a better example of being on both sides of the fence at the same time and being completely illogical. I think these two quotations from page 3640 of Hansard will go down in history in that respect.
Nor are the hon. member's figures any more dependable than his reasoning. The hon. member's statement that the parcel post rate changes will yield a revenue increase of $22 million is quite wrong. The revenue increase,

as previously reported and which is on record in Hansard and available to all, is $9.3 million. The hon. member was quoting the total revenues which the department received two years ago from the parcel post rate.
The hon. member said:
(Translation):
-parcel post rates have gone up 90 per cent.
(Text):
The English translation is:
... parcel post rates have Increased by 90 per cent.
The actual increase is 44 per cent. The hon. member says that the department's publication "Postmark" printed my picture 70 times. In 1960, even if you throw in all the members of parliament, my parliamentary assistant and myself, there were only 13 occasions on which our pictures appeared. More significantly, in 1960 some 1,642 postal employees' pictures appeared in our little magazine that is devoted to telling our staff what their far-flung organization is doing.
The hon. member for St. Denis said there was no French version of our public relations pamphlet "Letter Perfect". Such a version, which is an exact duplicate, is available on exactly the same basis and for the same purpose as the English one. I have it here, and I might mention in passing that to the best of my knowledge it was mailed to the hon. member with the same letter that went out to other hon. members of the house. I am looking at other hon. members over there and I am appealing to their honesty. They will know they received the French version of our pamphlet in the mail. Let them deny it.
The hon. member for St. Denis says that this year there were more thefts and more money involved in those thefts. In my opening remarks I pointed out that there were 295 post office break-ins in the past fiscal year as compared with 366 in the previous year. For the first 11 months cash and postage supply losses were down from $162,000 to $92,000, so the hon. member was wrong again.
There is no point in continuing with this recital of his discrepancies and errors, and I do not intend to do so. I merely point out that this is not a matter of differing opinions. This is a simple case of mathematics and facts being completely and absolutely wrong. His entire remarks with regard to the post office bristled with factual inaccuracies and wrong conclusions.
Now let me deal with a few of the other points raised by hon. members. First, automation and mechanization. We find that the Liberal party is against it. We find that the C.C.F. party favour it, each according to their remarks. We find the hon. member for St. Denis saying this on the subject:
Supply-Post Office (Translation):
He should at least wait until there is less unemployment before thinking about replacing men by machines.
(Text):
The translation is, and this is significant:
We should at least wait until there is less unemployment before thinking about replacing men with machines.
This is one of the fundamental differences between the hon. member for St. Denis and the whole Liberal party and myself and my party. We are looking ahead. Our work and our studies are not being carried out for the next two or three months; they are being carried out for years ahead. Our plans in the Post Office Department are for years ahead. The concept that you should wait until you are faced with a disastrous situation before doing anything about it, which is exactly the concept put forward by the hon. member for St. Denis, is of course completely wrong. The hard facts are that we have to think ahead. Machines must be developed if we are to continue our efficient operation with the increasing volume of mail and the increasing size of our cities. We must do this to keep postal rates reasonable and extend our services as members of parliament have asked us to do.
Look back over past history. We started off with men clearing letter boxes on foot and carrying the mail in bags over their shoulders. We mechanized with horses and wagons, and then with trucks. Do you want us to go back to the days of men clearing mail boxes on foot? We originally started off hand stamping every individual letter in order to cancel the postage stamp. Today we have machines for that purpose. Do you want us to go back to employing hundreds of people at rush times in the post office, who will be standing there stamping one letter after another and handling the mail? We used to have men carry bags from one point to another. It is a rough, difficult task. We put in conveyors to do it, to try to dignify people and free them to do other jobs which make a greater demand on their human intelligence.
I have no apologies to make for that sort of thing. Perhaps the best present example of how foolish is this argument against automation is that just within the past year, by the development of automated accounting processes, we have been able to pay our 8,000 revenue postmasters across this country twice a month instead of only once a month. This is something for which they have been asking for years and years. When I asked them if they would like to go back to a one pay a month system their remarks were not too complimentary, and I can understand why.

Supply-Post Office
On the one hand we have the Liberal party saying the postal workers are ill treated by the present administration and that their morale is low, and on the other hand we have the hon. member for Kootenay West, representing another party of the opposition with no better reason to favour this government, saying that in recent years there has been a great improvement in morale owing to improvements in administration and working conditions. I think we need go no further than to add the fact that postal employees today are better paid and better treated and receive better co-operation from management within the post office than ever before in our history, and that none of them are afraid of postal progress or automation.
Criticism has been levelled at the public relations department generally. I think basically this represents a misunderstanding of one of the major functions of this department. This is not a group designed to get publicity for the post office as such. It is what one might call a customer relations operation in very large measure. The majority of the personnel in the department spend their full time in centres across Canada working with postal users, ironing out special problems, leaving postmasters free to contemplate the day to day administration of their offices.
On the question of the deficit, our policy, enunciated originally and adhered to since, is to so operate the department as to break even on our over-all operation. The estimated $9 million deficit this year is really due to salary adjustments which ran throughout the entire year. There is no complaint about that; they are fair, reasonable and just. Next year when the changes in parcel post rates are in operation I confidently expect the department again to come close to, or reach, this breakeven point.
As far as the increase in parcel post rates is concerned, the opposition chose to criticise that as well, and I would remind them that this is the first increase in ten years. The amount of the increase has been very badly misrepresented; one hon. member said the increase amounted to as much as 100 per cent. In fact it represents an average increase of 44 per cent. One of our major actions was to remove a special rate which had previously existed within 20 miles of post offices. This concession had been introduced many years ago at a time when communications were not as good as they are today, and when many farmers were in the habit of doing their shopping by mail. In recent times this particular section of the rates was being misused by some of the largest mailers in Canada, who would bundle up their parcels and send them by freight or car to a particular post office, and thus serve a great mass

of people within 20 miles of that post office at a rate substantially below cost. The elimination of that rate will react to the benefit of the small shopkeeper and the small operator.
It must be remembered, too, that over the past ten years rail transport costs have gone up 120 per cent, and that our clerks are making 40 per cent more than they formerly did. There have been five rate increases by our competitors since the last one we put into operation. Finally, parcel post is still by far the cheapest way of sending parcels in Canada. I quote three rates as examples. A one pound parcel for delivery in the same province cost 10 cents under the old rate. The present rate in 23 cents and the corresponding express rate is $1. A five pound parcel sent three provinces away cost 67 cents under the old rate; the new rate is 84 cents, and the express rate is $1.07. A ten pound parcel sent to an adjoining province cost 89 cents under the old rate and $1.14 under the new rate. The express rate is $1.30. I still think that in the field of parcel post rates we have a most satisfactory and economic service.
Then, as to patronage, if you listened only to the words and overlook the examples you would think we were doing terrible things in this field. I tried to look into as many cases of this so-called patronage as I could. In one case I found that the man was operating a bakery and intended to go on operating it. He could not be a postmaster if he was operating a bakery full-time. How can a man bake bread and be able to serve the public in another capacity at the same time? In a number of other cases, including one at Trail, I found that these were straight civil service appointments made by the civil service commission, and if anyone wishes to question the integrity of the civil service commission he is free to do so, though I think it would be regrettable. The hon. member for St. Denis complains because we dismissed a postmaster for signing the nomination papers of a provincial candidate. Well, everyone of us knows that the signing of nomination papers very definitely places you on one side of the political fence as one of that man's supporters. We are not prepared in the department for that to be done.
The hon. member for Timiskaming in this same patronage field got himself into a long and involved discussion concerning a post office in Haileybury. I myself tried to find the newspaper account in the Toronto Telegram of March 14 which was supposed to report this incident. I went through every edition of the Telegram of that date, and the report is not there, Mr. Chairman. I looked at the Northern News, which he also purported to quote from, and I could not find

it there although I admit there were two pages torn out of that newspaper. Certainly it is not on record in the library. I finally sent my secretary to see the hon. member for Timiskaming but he could not produce any clippings either.
Actually I have nothing to say about the subject, except that it does not seem to have any foundation whatsoever. That is the sort of case that is supposed to have been made against us, and against me personally, contending that patronage is being practised in this department. In the Post Office Department we make something approaching 1,000 appointments every year, 850 of them, give or take a few, being made on my own authority as Postmaster General. Those who carp about patronage machinations on our part can only come into this house with about three or four trumped up incidents, every one of which can be immediately thrown out as having no effect. That is all I have to say about that subject.
I am not going to follow up, because I am not an expert-

to 35 communities. The cost involved there alone would be somewhere between $1 million and $1,500,000. We are not discarding the idea by any manner of means, but when an expenditure of that volume is in prospect I feel it is certainly something deserving further consideration.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam seemed to feel that small post offices were being eliminated in order to enlarge metropolitan post offices. This is not done as a matter of policy or choice. It does happen on occasion, when it must be done in the interests of efficient mail service. He criticized the Vancouver tunnel, a favourite subject of his. It was built under the preceding administration. It is not as effective as it was hoped it would be, but it is still a project which will bring savings, paying for its cost in about 20 years, so the presumptions he made in that regard were quite wrong.
The hon. member had much to say about Pitney-Bowes of Canada Limited. I can briefly say that it is not the only company in Canada in the postal meter machine business. There are a number of other machines in operation; Commercial Controls Canada Limited have one, the Friden Calculating Machine Company have another. There is another one called Postalia, and one called Neo-Post. This is not a monopoly field. In so far as we are concerned we rent certain equipment from this company merely because we feel it is cheaper from our point of view than to purchase them.
The hon. member for Port Arthur referred to second class mail rates. There is not much for debate in this regard until we are in possession of the O'Leary commission report. The fact remains, however, that the attitude not only of this government but of the preceding government in regard to second class rates has been that they are a concession designed to encourage the circulation of reading material which otherwise might not be circulated, and to that extent we can see value here. In answering another suggestion of his, I might say there is no doubt the post office has made progress as a result of decentralization.
In respect of progress, I would like to express my own personal appreciation to the president of the Canadian postmasters association who, when he introduced me last night, made the following statement, and I am reading from today's Journal. He is reported as saying:

Mr. Hamilton had done more for his department than any of his predecessors.
I appreciate that remark and commend it to the attention of the hon. member for St. Denis.

Supply-Post Office
The hon. member for Port Arthur suggested that we stop the passage of newspapers carrying football pool results because there is some connection, at least in his mind, between these football pool results in newspapers and the prohibition against playing the football pools. If we stopped every newspaper that carried news of anything illegal very few newspapers in Canada would move at all.

May I ask the minister a question. Has the minister checked as to whether those are advertisements in the newspapers in relation to illegal matters or whether they are published as news? I agree with him if they are published as news, but if they are advertisements, surely they represent an encouragement to an illegal enterprise.

will deal with that question later if the hon. member wishes. However, our view is that we cannot check individual advertisements in newspapers. We are not censors; that is the point I am making in this connection.
Finally the member for Port Arthur referred to the advertising of a certain type of commodity. This, of course, relates, as does everything we do, to whether it is legal or illegal in the eyes of the law. In this particular case the actions of one of the companies are under judicial review at the moment, and I think I would be getting into dangerous territory if I discussed this subject now.
The hon. member for Edmonton West urged that some consideration be given to providing carrier service in new subdivisions. I can only say to him that I feel we have gone a long way in this direction in recent years. We no longer require that there be sidewalks as such, but require only satisfactory walking conditions on a year-round basis. We do not even require that the streets be paved.
The hon. member for Kootenay West asks for assurance that there is no overlapping or duplication between the engineering and development branches of the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works. I certainly can give him that assurance without hesitation. That hon. member raised a number of other questions which I will deal with perhaps in correspondence, because I feel they are detailed and of interest primarily to him.
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception was worried about wages paid in St. John's, Newfoundland, at Christmas time. Perhaps the most satisfactory answer is that the dollar that was paid there is exactly the same dollar rate which was paid for similar work in other post offices in Canada. We treat our

employees in St. John's on the same basis as we treat employees in any other area. Because I have great love for the hon. member for Trinity-Conception I treat him sometimes a little better than others.
The hon. member for Timiskaming inquired about examinations for grade III individuals in our district offices. Perhaps the short answer to that question is there are no examinations for grade III individuals in district offices. Those of our employees who do have to take examinations in regard to their distribution knowledge must procure their own equipment. This equipment is not particularly costly, but the introduction of it for our employees in Canada would cost something over $50,000. We have not discarded that idea entirely; as a matter of fact we have it under review at the present time.
The hon. member also asked about our intentions with respect to highway post offices. We have no expectation at the moment of entering into the field of highway post offices. There are two reasons for this. First, we find that our existing system of highway services using trucks on which the mail is carried but not sorted is eminently successful. Second, we have noticed with great interest that the United States, which entered this field on a fairly extensive basis, is now in the process of drawing back and eliminating a great many of its highway post offices. In addition, to the best of our knowledge they have no plans for the building of any new vehicles or anything of that kind.
The hon. member asked about the reduction in railway post offices, those that travel along the rails. I remind him that we do not eliminate railway post offices by choice. We have been forced into it by the advent of the rail diesel car and changed services of the railways which leave us no other course. As of the 31st of March in each of the following years, the number of railway post offices in operation was as follows: in 1957, 126; in 1958, 108; in 1959, 96; in 1960, 78 and in 1961, 65. It seems to be bottoming out somewhat but generally speaking we have no other choice in this field when the railways reduce their services.

will only be about two minutes more and I am grateful to hon. members for their consideration. The hon. member for Westmorland referred to letter carrier service. When we introduce letter carrier service and make it available to a community we require that at least 80 per cent of the houses be equipped

with mail boxes, numbers on the front doors and so on. He suggested that the requirement be reduced to 65 per cent. When I came into the picture the requirement was actually 90 per cent and the point he raised applied then. A small portion of a community could deprive the entire community of letter carrier service, but 80 per cent seems to be about right. In most cases we can get the service into operation within a few weeks of its announcement. If we drop below that percentage very much, say to 65 per cent as he suggested, we are going to have the letter carrier bringing back to the post office about 35 per cent of the mail he takes out. This, of course, is not a satisfactory situation.
Many other points were raised which in almost every case involved details. If it is agreeable, I should like to follow the practice of previous years, one which I introduced, of giving the member concerned a lot of information in the form of a letter directly to the member. Otherwise we could take more time in the committee than hon. members would perhaps like to see taken on these matters. On the other hand, if a member wants to pursue on the floor of the house any particular matter that is of interest to him, I am ready, the officials are in the gallery, and we will certainly do everything we possibly can to try to assist hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief. A while ago I heard the minister state how concerned he was about the welfare of the employees in the post offices and I should like to deal with one matter relating to the Ottawa post office. As the minister knows, in other large cities such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver the senior employees work the day shifts and those junior to them work the evening and night shifts. The employees of the Ottawa post office have voted three times on this matter. The votes were not suggested by the employees themselves but were requested by the department. The circular relating to the matter says that the decision is to be based on the preference of the majority of the employees.
As I stated, there have been three votes in Ottawa in favour of the senior men having the day shift and the juniors the evening and night shifts just as is the case in all other large cities. For some reason or other, however, the department has refused to abide by the decision. I think this is rather unfair, and the reasons invoked by the department are not very good. Some suggestion was made that everybody did not vote. I suppose it is questionable whether some of us would be sitting in this chamber if everybody in our ridings voted.

quite agree with the hon. member and I will first look into the matter myself. As I am in Ottawa I can do that. We will see what the situation is and if we can meet the wishes of the employees in matters like this and there are no good reasons for not doing so we will certainly do so.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to advise the committee that I wrongly informed hon. members the other day, as found on page 3686 of Hansard, in relation to the examinations taken by clerks. I obtained my knowledge of the matter recently and I believe that the minister was not fair to those who are interested in this matter by making the references he did as he was probably well aware that I was referring to grade IV and not grade III clerks. Grade I, grade II and grade IV clerks take these examinations but grade III clerks do not. The remarks and suggestions I made at that time related to grade IV clerks.
I have since made inquiries and I find that these examinations are not nearly as simple a matter as might be thought at first. I talked to an employee the other day who told me that originally three or four hundred hours are involved in learning the procedure and therefore, particularly in the sorting section, this is not a simple examination. While it is true that it may take only 20 or 30 hours a year for a man to keep up to date, three or four hundred hours of work are involved in the first instance and the remuneration of $150 semi-annually is not a very large amount of money to compensate for the extra training they have to undergo.
I have already read to the committee an extract from the Northern News of March 14,

Supply-Post Office
1961 and referred to certain letters that are applicable to the matter in question. The other day one hon. member asked me about this matter but unfortunately he is not here now. I told him that when I went home over the week end I would see the reporter. I said I had received telephone calls from Toronto because of the communication that had been sent to the Telegram by the staff reporter. I spoke to the editor of the Telegram and made known certain views that I hold with respect to this matter. I told the hon. member who asked me for confirmation of what I had said that I would see the reporter in question and would get a copy of the communication for his information.
I am not in any position to find anything in the Telegram. I seldom read that particular daily newspaper. I am told there are several editions of it published to cover various areas. 1 have been assured by the reporter from the Toronto Telegram that this item, at least in part, appeared in the newspaper that day.
May I say that I was surprised at the strength and vigour exhibited by the minister in pursuing this matter. I was surprised also at something else. I give him much less credit than I thought I would have to give him in respect of the question I asked him in relation to the establishment of post offices. I am still curious about this. Was I wrong in my supposition that before a post office is established experts are sent to assess the situation; that the Postmaster General receives briefs from various organizations demanding this type of service, either through an M.P. or some other means? Is it not true that the minister has these people who go to assess the situation from the point of view of the mailing facilities that are available and the financial arrangements that may be necessary before an office can be established? I feel it is more important to have a statement that this is the course followed than to have a strong disavowal that patronage is taking place. People are interested in learning just how to go about getting a post office. Many of them are of the opinion that patronage is the only method of obtaining this service.
I shall read the copy of the telegram.
Ontario Northland Communications Telegram
Haileybury (March 14, Ray De Souza)-A federal milding for Haileybury? A department of public works or an unemployment insurance commission branch here?
These are the things which C. Foster Rice, Timiskaming's defeated Progressive Conservative candidate in the late federal election is willing to take up with Ottawa. However, he wants letters from the Haileybury chamber of commerce and town council to back him up on his trip to the capital.
Last night council unanimously approved a resolution calling on town clerk Frank Haskett to

request Mr. Rice to pursue the matter of obtaining a federal building for Haileybury.
Councillor Mary Lavigne said the new building if erected here could house a post office and possibly a department of public works as well as a branch office of the unemployment insurance commission.
Mayor Arthur H. Cooke, councillor Ben Budgeon and Mr. Lavigne confirmed they had been advised by national P.C. organizer Grosart to deal with the federal government through the defeated Conservative candidate rather than through Arnold Peters, C.C.F. member of parliament for Timis-kaming.
Councillor Ken Buflam thought Mr. Peters was due for some courtesy in the matter as a sitting member.
"It might be simpler to get in through the back door," Mr. Lavigne stated. "Mr. Peters handling the matter might do us more harm than good."
"Here we have a riding lost by 210 votes," the mayor commented. "All we have to do is what has been recommended."
Mr. Rice recently unsuccessfully sought action from government on waterfront improvements at Haileybury. Mr. Cooke said the government did nothing about the defeated P.C. candidate's request then.
Council did not authorize Mr. Haskett to forward a copy of the resolution to Mr. Peters.
I did not make my statement nearly as strong as this telegram because I was making it from reports that I had heard. However, I would ask, who is Mr. Grosart? What authority has he got to go around the country telling people to disregard the democratic processes that are involved in this matter? Is Mr. Grosart the man who runs the Post Office Department? I think we already have had the answer of the Postmaster General who has O.K.'d this post office. What we are asking now is, does he O.K. what Mr. Grosart says or does he O.K. the establishment of a post office because certain prerequisite conditions have been met?
I have no objection, Mr. Chairman, to Mr. Rice coming to Ottawa and asking for anything he can get for my constituency and his friends in that riding. We are both residents of that riding and we both want to get as much as possible for it. I have not really any objection to the town council doing what they wish. However, Mr. Chairman, the situation in the town of Haileybury is a disgrace. We are renting a post office in that town which I do not think is a credit to any town one quarter the size of Haileybury. The town of Haileybury is an up and coming community, and I believe it has a right to expect a much better post office than it has.
Let me relate what has happened with regard to the post office in Haileybury. A number of years ago the postmaster in that town was a gentleman by the name of Hamilton. When Mr. Hamilton died his estate took over the property that belonged to him, namely the post office. The Hamilton estate sold the post office to a Mr. Cooke who is

now the postmaster but he has no qualifications whatever for operating a post office. He has a staff of three who operate the office. I am told that Mr. Cooke has no formal training and does not have to take an examination before receiving an appointment as his employees do.
Mr. Cooke is also the mayor of the town. It is not surprising to me that Mr. Cooke has never written to me, as his federal member of parliament, on behalf of the council requesting a new post office because if the town of Haileybury gets a new post office he probably will not be the postmaster. He will be no longer renting the building to the postal department, a fact which gives him the opportunity of being the postmaster. I do not want it to be said that I am opposed to Mr. Cooke himself, and I can see that this type of arrangement has some advantages to it. However, I do not believe it is an arrangement that should be perpetuated.
I have in my hand a copy of a civil service circular which gives notice that a postmaster is required at Elk Lake, Ontario. Under the heading "Qualifications", there is a note to the effect that the postmaster will be required to provide the necessary postal premises. Second, the successful candidate will not be required to give his constant attention to the duties of the position. Unlike the situation to which the Postmaster General referred a few minutes ago, this job will allow him to operate his bakery on almost a full-time basis and he will also be able to operate the post office. The Postmaster General does not need to worry because there is not a bakery that large in the town of Elk Lake. However, we seem to be perpetuating a situation that is causing a great deal of difficulty in the Haileybury area.
I think one of the problems that may be involved here may be the fact that the citizens themselves have been so badly misinformed in the past by the politicians. Certainly, they are being misinformed by Mr. Grosart at the present time. In my opinion, Mr. Grosart should not be in a position to speak for the Postmaster General and make this kind of commitment. Misinformation is going out to the effect that post offices are obtained by means of political patronage. I think I agree with the Postmaster General, and I hope this is his opinion, that post offices are not obtained in this manner. Certain conditions have to be met, and political considerations are not a factor. If this is not true, then this civil service circular to which I have referred should not be sent out by the civil service commission but should be sent out by the defeated candidate. The defeated candidate would be able to appoint the postmaster in this particular town.

I have no reason not to believe that political patronage, in that old fashioned sense, is gone from these appointments. I think this sort of thing is a disservice when we put a man in as head of a municipality. Here are three councillors and the reeve of the municipality who have met with the national organizer of the Conservative party and have been told these things. They obviously are going to take his word because he is from out of town. He also gave them, I am sure, certain assurances. They are going to take his word and this is the word that is going to be distributed and disseminated throughout the area, namely that these things are accomplished in this manner.
I raise this matter only because it seems to me that in this regard democracy can be ill served and that the ends of justice that are inherent in democracy cannot be served if this type of talk is not stopped, and it is not patronage; it is only talk. If this kind of suggestion is not removed from our political scene, then if we look the other way and do not mention it, we are doing a disservice to the cause of democracy that is almost as great as the disservice done by these people that are promising it.
I should like the Postmaster General to rise in his place and indicate just what method will have to be followed in the case of Haileybury if they are going to receive favourable consideration in respect of a post office in that town.

I answer the hon. member very briefly. I say first that any suggestion that Mr. Grosart or anyone influences the department in its decisions is completely unfounded. Certainly if Haileybury or any other town feels that they would like a post office, let them write to the department and we shall be delighted to go into the matter with them. The probability is that in most cases, as many communities know to their satisfaction, before they get around to writing we will already be in there in co-operation with the Department of Public Works and building a post office.

I listened with great interest to the comments of the minister. I am sure he will bear with me if I mention two matters which really are not new to him but which cause some of us a good deal of concern. One is the matter of salaries paid to postmasters and postmistresses in some of the small communities in Newfoundland. I am thinking of course, of the small communities in my own district of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador.
I readily agree that the revenue in these post offices is small and that if the salary is based upon the revenue, then the salary must of necessity be small. I think, however,

Supply-Post Office
that below a certain sum salaries should cease to be the yardstick and that service should then be the means of measuring remuneration. Postmasters and postmistresses are necessary even in small places. The work takes a considerable portion of their time. It demands their presence in the post office. It means they must find a place to operate the post office business. If they are carrying out an essential service and if the revenue from that service is small, certainly it would be a great mistake to take the sum of that small revenue and use it as a basis for salary. As I said, below a certain level, service should be taken as a yardstick for payment rather than revenue. In other words what I am pleading for is a minimum wage for postmasters and postmistresses.
The other point I wish to make is in connection with mail service in northern Newfoundland in what I might generally refer to as the St. Anthony area. During the winter the service is faster than it is in summer because the air mail service is satisfactory and gives a much more regular and rapid service than that which is given in the summer time when the mail is carried by ship. During the season-shall I say the shipping season-when the post offices are served by the coastal steamers, mail deliveries are infrequent. I am told that it is not unusual for a period of two weeks to elapse between the time a letter is mailed and the time it is received. I refer to a letter, say, from the mainland. It would not take very long to get from here to Newfoundland by air but the time is used up by the slow steamship service.
This is a matter which I have brought to the attention of the minister and I agree with him that an air mail service all the year around is expensive. What I wanted to suggest now is that he might consider a limited air mail service during the summer months for first class mail only with a limited number of flights. I am sure that this procedure would improve the service. It could be the case that the cost may be out of proportion to the service rendered, but such a service is really necessary. I should like the minister to give this matter consideration, and I will limit my request to the possibility of a limited service confined to first class mail by air in the northern communities of Newfoundland.
In conclusion I should like to thank the minister for his program of sending mail by road and, wherever possible, with greater frequency or more mails per week. I know that in a number of places which ask that services be increased from one mail to two or three mails per week, it has been done. In
[Mr. Granger.!
thanking the minister I would express the hope that he will continue to pursue that program and enlarge it.

Very briefly, Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention something that the minister could perhaps mull over for the next two years and give an answer say in 1963. With the approach of confederation centennial ceremonies in 1967, it strikes me from perhaps a limited study, that there is only one real opportunity available to commemorate higher education in this country during that time. The year 1964 will be the 175th anniversary of the founding of the oldest university in the commonwealth. I refer to the University of King's College in Halifax. While 175 may not be as convenient an anniversary as say 200 or even 100, nevertheless I think it would be most fitting if the Postmaster General could at least consider the suggestion that one of his excellently designed fine stamps be issued to pay homage to higher education in this country. I therefore turn his thoughts to a fine ancient and honoured institution in my own riding of Halifax.

The Postmaster General did not reply to some of the questions I asked the other day. They were not personal questions. I thought they were questions of general interest and I am going to repeat them. But before I do so I want to reply to some of the things the minister said this afternoon in replying to criticisms that have been made of his estimates.
The Postmaster General said that one of the chief criticisms that had been levelled at him was for having pride in his department. I do not think anybody would criticize the minister for being proud of his department. We all pay tribute to the staff of the post office and their dedication to their various duties.
I think most hon. members criticize the fact that the Postmaster General perhaps seemed inclined to take a little too much credit unto himself rather than give it to the staff of the post office. As I listened to his performance I thought he was inclined to be a little truculent and at times was perhaps talking with his tongue a little bit in his cheek.
We do not take exception to that. I think this helps to liven our procedure. However, I do not think the Postmaster General should take too much exception to that kind of criticism. We want to assure the Postmaster General that we are all proud of the post office. We are all proud of his staff and their achievements. However, we do not want

the Postmaster General to create the impression that the post office came into existence when he took over two or three years ago.
That is very good.

I think that is implied in some of the remarks made by the Postmaster General in reply to the statements of the hon. member for St. Denis. He labelled the hon. member for St. Denis and the Liberal party with being against progress. He said we are the people who want to go back to the system of delivering mail on foot and manually cancelling the stamps one at a time, and all these other crazy things.
That is what the hon. member said.

The Postmaster General represents a party that has entered the electronic age and gone up into outer space along with the Russian astronaut. However, mechanization did not begin with this Postmaster General coming into office. It did not begin with the Tory party. It has been going on in the post office, as a gradual development, ever since the post office was created.
Progress was made under the Liberal regime and I am glad to see it being continued. However, we do not want the Postmaster General to try and create the impression in the country and in this house that there was no progress under the Liberal party and the only progress has taken place during the past two or three years while he has been administering the Post Office Department.
If the Postmaster General had listened to his remarks today as I was listening to them he would have received exactly the same impression as I, that here again he was not being completely non-partisan in the way he was replying to our criticisms.
We can tolerate a little political give and take on this matter, but the Postmaster General must realize there is a limit to it. I think if he will take the trouble tomorrow to read what appears in Hansard-although in cold print it will be very different from the way it appeared when we listened to the spoken word-he will get the impression that he was guilty of the very exaggerations and excesses for which he criticized the hon. member for St. Denis in his speech the other day. In that respect the Postmaster General is perhaps the pot calling the kettle black.
We are making progress. Which is the hon. member for St. Denis, the pot or the kettle?

I asked the Postmaster General two or three questions and he did not

bother to reply. Perhaps he thought they were not important enough. They were not questions which applied specifically to my own riding; they were general questions which I thought would be of interest to the public at large.
One of those questions was: which was the most profitable to the post office from the standpoint of net revenue, the selling of postage stamps or the use of postage meters? I think that is a general question, because from the report we received it appears that the revenue from postal meters is increasing at such a rate that it is perhaps equal to, or even in excess of the revenue from the sale of postage stamps. If there is more expense in-

Let
us stop this discussion. I will tell you right now. It is postal meters.

All right. I asked that question but the minister did not see fit to make any reference to it. I asked another question in connection with the list of special categories. There was quite an increase for transportation of mail by land, air and sea. My question in relation to this matter was: was this increase due to more contracts, or to contracts that had been renewed at higher rates? That was also a question of public interest.
I asked one question to which perhaps the minister might wish to give an individual reply, and I would not press him to answer it in this committee. I refer to the question I raised with regard to putting out a special stamp issue for Christmas. Many prominent people in my province are interested in this matter and I hope the Postmaster General will give it favourable consideration.
After we had a chance to read and study what the Postmaster General said when introducing his estimates we of course were in a better position to ask questions. I think the Postmaster General not only fired our imagination but aroused our curiosity when he told us about the advent of these electronic, automatic mail handling machines.
I should like to ask several questions in connection with this matter. The first one is this: how much money has the Post Office Department invested in the development of this kind of equipment? My second question is: assuming that the equipment passes the test and becomes available, under what conditions does it become available to the post office, and under what conditions will it be manufactured? I ask this question because one can readily understand that this is a very special type of equipment with a very limited market and it is quite possible that its manufacture and distribution could be

Supply-Post Office
monopolized by a particular firm. I should like full details with respect to the whole procedure of developing and acquiring this kind of automatic, electronic equipment.
The Postmaster General told us the other day that 100,000 firms in Canada were now receiving twice a day delivery. That is fine. We hope it may be extended. However, I think most hon. members would like to have an answer to this question: on what basis are these 100,000 firms selected? Where does the Post Office Department draw the line between firms which rate two deliveries of mail a day and firms which rate only one delivery a day? These are all the points I wish to make at the present time, Mr. Chairman, but I will probably have other comments to make later on.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I must tell the minister that the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) could not be present this afternoon. He is the first to regret his absence, no doubt.
It is particularly unfortunate that the minister showed himself not only so cruel but so unfair toward the hon. member for St. Denis. Allow me to show at once in what way the minister was unfair in his remarks regarding the member for St. Denis. He said, in French and in English, that in the speech he made last week, the member for St. Denis stated the following:
I am all for progress, but I am against it-
And the minister suggested that the member for St. Denis would be the laughing stock of everybody for saying such a thing.
If we refer to page 3640 of Hansard for April 13, we note that the minister has been unfair to the member for St. Denis in that he did not quote the whole sentence. Here, in fact, is the textual quotation as it appears in Hansard:
I am all for progress, but I am against it when it is introduced at the expense of the human element, particularly in times of unemployment.
That is something else. I shall come back later to the matter of mechanization, but I fully endorse what the member for St. Denis had to say on this subject.
If the Postmaster General is so confident of the position he is taking in these difficult times to step up mechanization in the postal service to the extent of creating unemployment instead of providing jobs, as he should be doing with a greater volume of business, I am sure that on a matter of principle of such importance, at a time when the government, the first employer in the country, should be setting an example for private industry,

the hon. member for St. Denis, myself, or any other member of the island of Montreal, would be delighted during the next election campaign, to meet the Postmaster General in the riding of his choice, and we shall then leave it to the voters to settle the matter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the member for St. Denis is one of the most assiduous members in this house. I think he is celebrating this year the 25th anniversary of his election as a member, and since the second session of 1957 especially, he has shown a tremendous interest in the Post Office Department, never failing to raise matters of very great importance pertaining to that department. He has also made very interesting suggestions.
In my opinion, the speech delivered last week by the hon. member for St. Denis was remarkable; it was a speech that dismayed the Postmaster General, and the minister vainly tried today to minimize its impact.
Mr. Chairman, one may not particularly relish the sense of humour displayed by the hon. member for St. Denis when he is being critical, but if we had more members like him in this house, more members with the humour and the engaging personality of the hon. member for St. Denis, it would afford relief from the attitude of certain government members who, unfortunately, are always down in the mouth. I fail to see what the Postmaster General could gain for himself in trying to minimize a speech replete with figures and facts that are unquestioned.
Erroneous.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Denis-
He was wrong.

-gave facts and figures, and I would greatly appreciate it if the minister replied to this after a while. If those figures and those facts were erroneous, why did not the minister stand up at the time and ask the hon. member what was the basis for those facts and figures? The hon. member for St. Denis would then have been very pleased to inform the minister who seems to be quite unaware of some of the things that happen in his department.
I wanted to ask questions, but the hon. member for St. Denis asked me to wait till he was finished.

speechtext: That is true.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is right. I was in the house at the time,

but why did not the Postmaster General ask his questions after the member for St. Denis had concluded his remarks? I am sure the hon. member for St. Denis would have considered it a pleasure to reply.
Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General seems to think we are all being rather hard on him. He has been asking for it. As I said one day, he who sows the wind shall reap the whirlwind. For two or three years, the Postmaster General promised two mail deliveries a day. He promised them even to his constituents in Notre Dame de Grace; yet, he said not a word about it in the statement he made in introducing his estimates. He said not a word about thefts. The member for St. Denis quoted figures which the minister should not be denying. I hope the minister will not force me to read those I have here. I can read them if he wants me to, but I am sure he will not deny them. Those figures show that in the last year, there have been more thefts than in 1957. I hope the minister will not deny this.
With regard to compensation claims for registered mail or insured parcels, the number of claims in 1956-57 was 11,800, as against 13,020 in 1959-60. I do not think the minister will deny these figures. How much money did such compensation claims involve? For 1956-57, $128,202; for 1959-60, $170,134. Some of the money has been recovered; in fact, an amount of $11,281 was recovered in 1956-57, and in 1959-60, the figure was $11,442. Where is the improvement there? These figures cannot be denied.
Mr. Chairman, I raised no objection when the minister told us a moment ago that the publication about which the hon. member for St. Denis raised such a fuss had been translated into French. I cannot say, I have never received it. The hon. member for St. Denis has not received it, nor have I, nor has the member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier). We did get the English version, and that is what the member for St. Denis stated.
With regard to patronage, here is the statement made by the hon. member for St. Denis as recorded on page 3640 of Hansard for April 13:
I will mention two or three cases only, without going into all the details. If the minister wants more details, I am prepared to give them to him.
When did the minister accept the challenge? Never. I too, have dealt briefly with this matter of patronage.

The hon. member asked about the requirements for two deliveries a day. I think the easiest way to deal with this is to say we have four classes of letter carrier walks. First, there is the residential class which comprises those with less than 25 per cent business calls. In this instance we give one delivery a day to all calls. Second, there are mixed walks, those with 25 per cent to 50 per cent business calls, with regard to which we give twice a day delivery to the businesses and once a day to the residences. Third, there are the business walks, those with over 50 per cent business calls. In this case we give two deliveries per day to businesses-sometimes more if the volume of mail warrants it-and once a day delivery to residences. Then, we have, finally, the residential-business type of walk which we develop when it is in the interests of improved postal service to business. With this multiple delivery walk we are able to serve businesses twice a day and residences once. I think that perhaps answers this question.
