To
the best of my knowledge there is no fixed rule. I know from experience that generally we prefer people who have done this work before and there certainly is a tendency on the part of postmasters interested in operating as efficiently as possible to engage applicants who had had past experience.

I wish to say just a few words, briefly, about a matter which is of local interest in my constituency, but before doing so I should like to say to the Postmaster General that when he came to Windsor recently to officiate at the opening of the new addition to the post office he extended to me a courtesy which I greatly appreciated. I told him so at the time, and I want to repeat it now because I am grateful for the fact that when he was in Windsor, a distinguished visitor in one of Canada's dynamic communities, he extended to one of the members of parliament who did not share his political views the kind of courtesies which I think are proper and I want him to know that I appreciate what he said.
I neglected to say to the minister on that occasion what I should like to say to him in this committee now, namely that I am sure the records of the department will show that the former member for Essex West, the late Donald Brown, played a great part in arranging under the former administration for the planning which came to fruition with the completion of this addition. I am not taking credit away from anyone who is contemporary, but I do think that in fairness to the memory of that very active public servant and member of parliament, the citizens of Windsor and Essex county generally would appreciate a word in recognition of what he had done with regard to the extension to the post office in Windsor.
However, I rise at this time primarily to ask the minister to give consideration to a
Supply-Post Office
matter which I have raised from year to year, and that is the desirability now of giving consideration to the establishment of a post office building in one of the thriving communities of the constituency I have the honour to represent. I refer to the community known as Belle Riviere. That community lies along the shore of lake St. Clair. It has a volume of business now and an importance in the county generally which, I think, warrant special consideration being given to it. I hope the minister will find my words today-words which paid him a tribute which I combined with my request-something of an inspiration to accept the proposal I am asking him to recognize. I hope he will use his good offices with the Minister of Public Works and recommend to him the desirability of building a post office in Belle Riviere.
While he is doing that, as I think he will, I would ask him also to give consideration to the desirability of establishing a post office building now in the township of Sandwich East in Essex county which has assumed by virtue of the increase in the population an importance which I am sure the records of the department will confirm. These are matters which do not seemingly have the importance of some of the subjects which the minister was discussing today but I can assure the hon. gentleman that they are matters of considerable importance in the communities to which I have referred.
I close what I have to say by observing that I thought the minister was a little harsh on the hon. member for St. Denis. I do not think this house suffers from the good humour of the hon. gentleman from St. Denis. I think he has served in this chamber as a very constructive critic of the important department of government over which the hon. gentleman presides. I do not think the minister should be too touchy. He should not resent the kind of criticism which comes from the hon. gentleman, generally with a smile and a touch of humour which has endeared him to all members. After all, the hon. member for St. Denis is a distinguished member of this house. He has been a member of this parliament since 1935 and anyone who has had the long period of public service that he has had certainly qualifies for the succession in a year or so following the next federal election. I have no right to say who the next postmaster general will be in the next Liberal government but I would suspect from the contributions which the hon. member for St. Denis has made that he would have a very strong claim by virtue of his distinguished record as a critic of the Post Office Department during the time the hon. gentleman has been Postmaster General and during the time the present government has been in office.

Supply-Post Office
I hope the Postmaster General, before he leaves that post either to become deputy minister or upon the resignation of the present administration, will take steps to have a post office built by the shores of lake St. Clair in Belle Riviere and also to establish the kind of building in Sandwich East which I think the situation warrants. When the opening of the post office in Belle Riviere takes place and the opening of the post office building in Sandwich East takes place, as I suspect will occur, I not only hope but know that the Postmaster General will extend to me, in the opening of these buildings, the same courtesy which he so generously extended the other day when he visited the city of Windsor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Now that the hon. member has started so well perhaps he would like to mention the rest of the cabinet that he proposes to bring in.
As we are dealing with each department of government I will be very glad to mention them.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Postmaster General listened with a great deal of interest and concern to the comments made by the hon. member for Essex East, but I hope in the interests of the citizens of Windsor and area he will not be influenced by the remarks made by that hon. member regarding the next election.
At page 3221 of Hansard for March 22, the Acting Secretary of State gave an answer to a question I had asked. The question was:
1.	How many days elapsed between the mailing of Hansard from the Queen's printer and the day to which the mailed Hansard applies?
2.	By what class of mail is Hansard mailed?
3.	What is the length of time that it takes for Hansard when mailed from the Queen's printer to travel to Vancouver?
The Secretary of State answered as follows;
1.	One working day.
2.	Third class.
3.	Normally three and a half or four and a half
days.
I have since that time received communications from individuals who subscribe to Hansard regarding the time it takes for Hansard to reach them.
I received one letter from Captain Baker, a Canadian citizen who, for reasons of health, is living in San Diego, California. He said he noticed the question and answer appearing in Hansard and felt that he should supply me with some information in this regard. The letter is dated April 17, and he mentions that 6 days previous, which would be April 11, he made an examination at his local post office and found that one copy of Hansard reached him 21 days after it was printed. He said that the assistant postmaster came right to his home with a bundle of four copies

of Hansard which had just arrived. He informed me that, together with the assistant postmaster, they opened them and tagged the covers which they mailed to Washington so that the officials there could make an appraisal regarding the United States postal system. I mention this as an example of the long period of time which elapses between Hansard being printed and delivered. I think hon. members will agree that 21 days is a rather long time for mail originating in Ottawa to be delivered in San Diego.
I received another letter from a Mr. B. L. Cope of Roberts Creek, British Columbia. Roberts Creek is a few miles north along the coast from Vancouver. This individual also subscribes to Hansard and noticed the question and answer. He listed in his letter a number of dates of Hansard and the time that elapsed between printing and delivery to him at Roberts Creek. The copies of Hansard mentioned are from March 1 to March 23, inclusive. I do not know that it would be in order for me to read the tabulation as it appears in the letter but I would be happy to do so or make it available to the minister. In any event this tabulation shows that one copy of Hansard took five days to reach him, five copies took six days, three copies took seven days, four copies took eight days, one took nine days, two copies took ten days, and one took 11 days. I feel this information is at great variance to that given by the Acting Secretary of State in reply to my question. If one allows even a day or two more than the four and a half days, as suggested in that answer, that is still a reasonable length of time, but an eight to 11 days' time lapse does not indicate efficient operation on the part of postal services.
I might mention that the gentleman in San Diego indicated also that some copies of Hansard had taken nine and 12 days to reach him. I would suggest that the information I have presented would warrant a thorough examination of the postal system on the part of the Postmaster General particularly in regard to the delivery of Hansard. I would also suggest that this situation exists in respect of other classes of mail.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I had completed my initial comments about the two letters I had received concerning the delivery of Hansard through the mail and the long

delay which exists in transporting Hansard from the Queen's printer to the subscriber through the postal system. I am sure the minister will take a look at this matter even though I know he has had a number of letters from interested individuals which apparently have resulted in no great speeding up in the delivery of Hansard through the mail.
I should like to raise another matter at this time in which I am sure each member of the committee has a personal interest. I refer to the franking privilege of members so far as the receipt of mail free of charge is concerned. During the time that the house is in session there is no difficulty, of course, but people do get into the habit of sending their mail to members without stamps. I am sure that other members as well as myself receive letters during the recess which do not have postage affixed on them and this results in double postage occasionally having to be paid. While I am not advocating the wholesale use of the frank from any post office in Canada throughout the year, I think that members' incoming mail should at least be transported free of charge during the time that the house is in recess. I understand this is a statutory matter and that an amendment to the legislation would be required. However, I think it would be a most welcome move if the minister would undertake to take this small step and thus save at least some members of parliament the few pennies in double postage that they have to pay from time to time.
I have another comment or two I should like to make. One has to do with a stamp album which I have not seen myself but which was described to me in the most glowing terms by a stamp collector. He received it as a gift from a friend who had travelled on the mainland of China. Apparently these albums are made available to philatelists through the postal system in Peking; at least that is where he said his friend obtained it. I would not attempt to describe it as he described it to me but apparently he felt it was a most worth-while type of album in that it was well prepared, was beautifully coloured and the inside pages did not provide for the usual arrangement of affixing stamps by gummed tabs but rather contained a series of folded plastic holders with slits in which stamps could be inserted and from which they could be removed without the risk of injuring the stamps in removing tabs. I think this is something which might be examined by the Post Office Department to see whether or not a similar type of service could not be provided to stamp collectors through the philatelic branch of the department. After all, attempts are made by this branch to see that first day of issue stamps and so on are made
Supply-Post Office
available to stamp collectors and the branch also looks after block sales of stamps to collectors. I think the service they render might be extended to the provision of albums of the sort I have described which would certainly be acceptable to those who collect stamps now and those who may take up the hobby in the future.
I have examined the report of the Postmaster General for the year ended March 31, 1960, and there are two or three questions I should like to pose to the minister with respect to the statement of revenue receipts found on page 42 of the report. I find that the income from the sale of meter and register impressions is almost equal to the income from the sale of postage stamps. In the case of postage stamps the total is $83.9 million in round figures and for meter and register impressions the total is $78.3 million.
I have not had occasion to look at past reports of the department but I am quite sure the income from the sale of meter and register impressions has been increasing substantially over the last few years because the use of postage meters has been increasing. I pose this thought to the minister, and I am sure this is a subject that will interest his colleague sitting next to him, the Minister of Justice, in that it may have some connection with operations under the Combines Investigation Act.
I am not sure of this, but I have been told that there is only one company in Canada, namely Pitney-Bowes, which makes and rents postage meters. I may be incorrect in that, but that is the information I have been given. If such is the case, it would appear to be obvious that Pitney-Bowes is in a monopoly position in so far as the manufacture and rental of postage meters is concerned. The rental arrangements which Pitney-Bowes enters into, of course, are based generally upon the amount of postage which goes through the meter. If Pitney-Bowes is the only firm in Canada which manufactures and rents postage meters or if it is the major firm and by virtue of its size has a monopoly in the field, then I feel some extensive investigation should be made to make certain the operations of this company do not contravene the provisions of the combines act or that the users of these meters are not overcharged.
If the minister has knowledge as to whether or not the Pitney-Bowes firm has a monopoly in this field, I would greatly appreciate a statement from him on the matter and also with respect to whether or not the department, either itself or in conjunction with the combines investigation branch, has made

Supply-Post Office
any inquiry into this particular aspect. Perhaps following that statement we may be able to discuss the matter to a larger extent, if not now then when the estimates of the Department of Justice are being considered.
There is another item on page 42 of the report under the statement of revenues and receipts which I should like to discuss. Toward the end of the item "receipts", there is an item "return on investments" which, during the fiscal year 1958-59 amounted to $10.9 thousand and for the year 1959-60 amounted to only $8.7 thousand. There has been a decrease in the return on investments. I should like to know what is the amount of the investment on which this particular return is received. Where does the money come from that is so invested, and in what securities is it invested? What is the interest rate that is payable on this investment?
I think those are a few of the items upon which I seek information. I realize the subjects are rather scattered but perhaps the minister, either now or later on, will obtain this information for me. Perhaps I should resume my seat at this time.

Perhaps I could deal with some of the points that have been raised until now, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Essex East was kind enough to indicate to us at least two points in his riding where he would like new buildings. We will be glad to have a look at these situations. I think perhaps the pleasant time we had in Windsor is an incentive to have him help us open new buildings, and I hope that similar arrangements will continue for some time to come.
The hon. member for Skeena referred to delays in the mailing of Hansard. While I have taken great pride in the operations of the department generally, I have always been very careful to point out that we are not perfect. It is very easy, I think, for any members of this house to bring forward specific instances of delayed mail. We like to know about these things. I would ask hon. members to let us know whenever they find an instance of mail being delayed.
We will certainly follow up this particular situation, although I might say if the situation is the one I think it is I have had a good deal of correspondence from this particular gentleman who resides outside of Vancouver. He is quite elderly and pays great attention to detail, but we do not always find the situation is exactly as it was represented. However, we will follow up this particular situation.
Franking, of course, as the hon. member pointed out is a statutory matter. We can have a look at the suggestion which he made, but it would certainly require a change in the

act. In so far as supplying albums is concerned, I would say right away that this is not a very attractive proposition so far as we are concerned. Our policy for our philatelic section has been to stay away from anything which competes directly in the commercial field. We do sell stamps because, after all, we do produce them. There is no appeal in entering the field of selling postage stamp albums and a number of such items in competition with private firms.
I put some information on the record this afternoon regarding Pitney-Bowes. There are a number of other firms in Canada that have postage meters available for rent and, in some cases, for sale. I believe I listed five such firms. We are delighted at any time to license anyone who manufactures a postage meter that meets our primary requirement, that is ensuring that the postage involved is protected and there is no possibility of fraud or loss. Pitney-Bowes, however, is the major operator in this field beyond any doubt. Beyond that, however, I think the hon. member suggested that he deal with the matter on the estimates of the Department of Justice and on behalf of my colleague the Minister of Justice, I take that item as notice.
Finally, the hon. member asked about the item "return on investments". This, of course, is an unusual item. Some government departments, but not too many, have investments. Many years ago the department, in cooperation with the postmasters across Canada, set up a postmasters' guarantee fund or a post office guarantee fund, I think, would be the proper term. This replaced what had previously been the situation under which postal employees and postmasters were bonded in various ways. The fund was derived originally from moneys assessed against people employed in the Post Office Department, primarily postmasters I would think although it was a fairly general assessment, but since 1919 no contributions have been required. At that time the fund had grown to approximately $300,000 and it was considered sufficient to meet any claims which might be made against it. The claims, of course, arise from defalcations on the part of individual postal employees who have been entrusted with sums of money.
We do not have at the moment any detailed list of the investments of this fund. However, if my memory serves me rightly, they are all government bonds of varying maturities and whatever interest is being paid on them is paid to the Post Office Department as such. I am delighted to say that the fund is increasing a little bit each year because of the fact that not too many claims are made against it owing to the honesty of our postal employees.

I might just mention in passing that this is a little item about which the Auditor General writes me periodically because he would like to see all the money nicely gathered into one central fund. We have stood firm on this matter, and so far have done so successfully, because we take the position that this money was contributed originally by postal employees and that we are not going to turn it over to one central fund. We want to maintain it separately because it is in their interests so to do.

I should just like to follow this matter along a bit, if I may, thanks to the graciousness of my colleagues. With respect to the delay in the mailing of Hansard, may I say that it was not a specific instance that was referred to me in this letter but rather a number of instances, as I have said, the ones he listed ranging from March 1 to March 23, inclusive. There are therefore perhaps 10 or 15 specific instances in which the times for the mailing of Hansard took longer than the normal three and a half days to four and a half days as announced by the Acting Secretary of State. However, as the minister said he would have a review made of this matter I will certainly give him the particulars that are contained in the letter so that they may be available to him.
I understand that the Post Office Department is also in the banking business and that it thereby competes with private industry in connection with savings and providing a service in that field. That does not seem to be too compatible with the idea of not wanting to compete in the commercial field in so far as stamp albums are concerned.
The minister mentioned the Pitney-Bowes Company as being the major company or, I think he said, by far the major company in the field of providing postage meters. I must apologize for not having been here at the time he mentioned the names earlier this afternoon. I wonder whether it would be possible for his department to provide information that would indicate the percentage of the market, as it were, that Pitney-Bowes and these other companies have in Canada, or whether it is possible to obtain that information in order that we may see how major Pitney-Bowes is in this particular field.
I shall pose a question to the minister with respect to outgoing mails as they are handled by the railway system. Again 1 have been told-and I have not had a chance to check on the matter-that outgoing mails are sent alternately via C.N.R. and C.P.R. from those communities which are serviced by those two railways when such mail is going to other communities which are also serviced by the same two railways. Otherwise the rail mail is
Supply-Post Office
shipped via the system which will go to that place if it is in fact served by only one railway. I wonder whether I have a correct understanding of the system, namely that the mail travels on alternate days or alternately anyway as between the two railroads in the circumstances I mentioned.

The
short question to this answer is no. There may very well be occasions on which the railways will have schedules that vary from day to day, perhaps a train which runs on Tuesday and Thursday, and there may be a different routing of that mail on the different days in order to make connections. I think a crossword puzzle, compared with the work of the transportation division, is very simple indeed because of the difficulty in connecting one link in moving mail with another. But basically, if a train is running regularly each day it is our practice to ship all the mail that is available by that train day after day. We do not alternate from one railroad line to another merely for the sake of alternating.

I am a little bit embarrassed tonight because I want to ask the minister for a service and I want to criticize the department. I do not know whether it is best to criticize the department and ask for the service afterwards or to ask for the service first and to criticize afterwards. I do not know which procedure will be the most effective.
Get to the point and save time. Be brief, whatever you do.
The hon. member should listen.
I hope I shall be able to make these remarks without having to listen to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi blowing his horn.
Brevity has its charms. I thought I would let the hon. member know.

The hon. member for St. Denis, when he made his remarks on the administration of the Post Office Department said that the minister was a brilliant one or rather, if I may correct myself, that the minister had made a brilliant report. The hon. member for Port Arthur said that it was not necessary for the minister to have his advisers at the table in front of him in order to make it possible for him to have his budget carried by the committee. I must admit that he is extremely efficient. In respect of some of the questions that he does not want to answer or for which he does not have the answer he says, "I will send it to you by mail". I think there are a great many questions that were asked here this afternoon the answers to which I would have preferred to get here

Supply-Post Office
rather than in the letter that is going to be sent to the hon. member who asked the question, inasmuch as it will probably be marked private and confidential and we shall probably never get to know what the answer is.
It is possible that the minister does not need his advisors in front of him in order to carry his budget in the committee. However, I think he should have some advisors in front of him when it comes to the matter of employer-employee relations. There is a low morale amongst the employees of the Post Office Department. I know the minister will probably deny that. Many of the employees who are not pleased with the treatment that they are getting in the depart-men do not wish to make official complaints.
That was prior to the raise.

That was prior to the raise. As a matter of fact they thought the raise was too long in coming. I do not think that the minister did any bodily harm to any of these fellows but I think he tried to worry them to death because he kept them waiting for two years. It lowered the morale of the department considerably. If the minister had taken the advice of the senior employees of the department I am sure that problem would have been settled before the expiration of two years.
As far as his personal administration is concerned and as far as he is responsible for making policy for the department I do not think there is so much to brag about when at the end of the year there is going to be a deficit of $9 million. It was, therefore, not in order to eliminate the possibility of a deficit that he kept the employees waiting two years. I think it was because the minister himself is of the opinion that he can run the Post Office Department without any assistance. All the employees of the Post Office Department who are trying to maintain the reputation which that department had prior to this present administration taking office, would perform their tasks in a much easier manner and would feel a great deal better about the situation, if the requests that they make for adjustments or the complaints they make with regard to working conditions were listened to and problems were solved much more quickly. I do not know whether the contagious habit of postponing decisions has affected the minister or whether the minister has affected the cabinet. For some reason or other a great many of these problems that should be solved are postponed and there is altogether too much procrastination.
This is what the employees of the Post Office Department have been comnlaining

about. They are not complaining openly because they are afraid of retaliation. I do not mean retaliation in the sense that they will lose their jobs, but retaliation in the sense that they will not get the promotion to which they are entitled, or the next time they ask for an adjustment in salary, instead of having to wait two years they may have to wait longer.
We do not behave like the Liberal government. Things have changed.

There is a boat in the canal again. I do not think anybody on this side of the house objects to mechanization. I was quite impressed by the statement of the minister that mechanization will not cause any post office employees to lose their jobs.
I know that mechanization is inevitable; we are going to have it. While it may not cause any of the present employees of the Post Office Department to lose their jobs, I am very much afraid that it will prevent other people from obtaining jobs which they should obtain. While mechanization should be gone into, I think it should not be gone into at an accelerated rate, but step by step so as to cause the least possible concern to the present employees of the Post Office Department and so as to bring about a partial solution to our present unemployment problem.
I think an employee or officer of the department should be appointed as a public relations officer. I do not mean a public relations officer to effect liaison with the people served by the Post Office Department, but with the people who serve the post office, the employees of the department.
I do not say that the minister does these things willingly. He is probably too busy. However, if there were an officer of that type to advise him, or if he were to listen to the senior officers of the department I am sure this would benefit not only the employees of the department but all the citizens of Canada.
I do not want the minister to forget what I have said, and I want him to clearly remember what I am now going to say.

You
have not said anything worth remembering.

The people of the town of Eastview have repeatedly asked for a post office. Eastview is a town of 25,000 people and I think they are entitled to this type of service. I have received many representations on this matter, the last one being from the Eastview board of trade, and I am told that no other town in Canada of this size is without a post office.
I urge most strongly upon the minister that he include a post office for the town of

Supply-Post Office
Eastview in the plans of the department this year. The people of Eastview feel they are being discriminated against as far as postal service is concerned. It is a town of 25,000 inhabitants as I said. Even if they are in close proximity to the city of Ottawa, it is very inconvenient at the moment for the people who live in Eastview to obtain in the city of Ottawa the type of service they require.
A post office in the town of Eastview would not considerably increase the deficit of the Post Office Department. I know the minister will take this matter into serious consideration and I hope this project will be accomplished without too much delay.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, at one time the city of Arthabaska, of which I am the humble representative as member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska, had as a resident the greatest statesman Canada has ever known, Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
There is in that city a post office of a very special character in that it is topped by an historic clock which the population wishes to keep as a souvenir of the good old days, of the years of prosperity and of pleasant memories.
I was told recently that it had been decided not to undertake certain repairs to the clock and to the belfry of that post office. I am told that the hands of the clock are gone, that the glass is broken, in a word that it needs a complete overhaul. On behalf of the citizens of the cities of Arthabaska and Victoriaville, and of the Arthabaska riding, I ask the Postmaster General whether he could not use $50 to $200 of his budget to make the necessary repairs and thus preserve that memento of the old days.
The city of Victoriaville will celebrate this year the centenary of its foundation and, in order to enhance the beauty of the city, we would like that clock to be repaired in order to show that the Conservative government is still functioning.

Mr. Chairman, I asked a question to the Postmaster General and I should like to get an answer.
(Text):

The
question of clocks in post offices is of course a matter for the Department of Public Works. I will draw it to the attention of my colleague. (Translation):
We shall do all we can so that the clock will work better in the future than it has in the past.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 308 carry?

Item agreed to.
309. Operations including salaries and other expenses of staff post offices, district offices, railway mail service staffs, and supplies, equipment and other items for revenue post office, including administration, $121,039,796.

Mr. Chairman. I do not wish to delay the passage of this item. I know the Postmaster General is anxious to have the item passed. However, I do want to support the remarks made this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. My colleague raised the question of a minimum salary for revenue postmasters. The Postmaster General pointed out that a minimum wage was already in effect, and I think he told us it was based on the volume of work carried out by the postmaster.
When the Postmaster General introduced his estimates the other day, in reply to a question I asked he said there had been a general increase in the salaries paid to revenue postmasters. I wish to make one observation and ask one or two questions in this connection.
The observation I wish to make is that "salary" does not seem to be a correct description of the payments to these revenue postmasters. It would have been a correct description a few years ago, but as I understand it, what the postmaster receives now could be more properly described as remuneration. It could more properly be described as remuneration because it includes not only a payment for his services but also an allowance for the provision of accommodation, fuel, lighting, maintenance, cleaning and other janitorial services.
In this connection I should point out to the Postmaster General that if this remuneration is based on the volume of work carried out, that is fine for the postmaster who has the post office located in his own residence or in some building of which he is the owner. However, in the case where the postmaster does not own the building, or where it is not in his own house and he has to pay rent being paid in accordance with the volume of work he carries out. He receives just the for the post office accommodation, he is not same payment as the man who handles the same amount of traffic and who can keep all the remuneration for himself because he owns the building in which the post office is housed.
The person who does not own the post office building and who handles exactly the same volume of work has to pay part of his remuneration to somebody else for renting

Supply-Post Office
the post office accommodation. That means an inequality in connection with people who are rendering the same service.
I wish to ask the Postmaster General a question, and perhaps he would prefer to reply by letter. I will not press him for a reply at the moment. The Postmaster General knows that in Newfoundland we have a special situation where the postmaster's salary is made up of two components one paid by the Post Office Department and the other by the Canadian National Telegraphs. In addition the question is still further complicated in that some of these salaries are subject to a ceiling and, I think, have been subsidized by both the post office and the C.N.T. In such cases any increases which may have been made in their pay would not be increases in fact because they would merely mean a reduction in the subsidies. Thus, the postmasters in this category will not be any better off.
I believe there are other cases where increases would only serve to lower the payments of the C.N.T. though I am not perfectly sure. The question I want to ask the minister is whether he would at some time let me have the number of post offices where the postmasters have not benefited at all from these increases. I should like him to tell me also what the minimum remuneration is at the present time and whether the increase was a straight across-the-board increase, and what the percentage rate of increase amounted to.

The
minimum salary for revenue postmasters at the present time is $245 per year for our smallest post offices. The increase which we gave the revenue postmasters was practically the same for all the grades although there were some variations to take account of certain special circumstances. Everything was rounded out to the nearest $5, as I remember.
And the approximate rate?

The
approximate rate is slightly higher, I think, than the average of the increases which have been granted to postal clerks. It has always been our practice to increase our revenue postmasters on the same basis as civil servants. There will always be circumstances which will vary cases but this is the practice we have followed in this case.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, from time to time it has been my privilege in this committee to consider the estimates of this department as well as the estimates of other departments from the position of a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. More recently it has been my privilege to take part in these important parliamentary discussions as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. On the first occasion I might be regarded as having been on the giving end of the firing line while on the second occasion I was in the second echelon as far as the receiving end is concerned. Tonight 1 find myself in the front line of parliamentary action for the first time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Which do you like best?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East has inquired which I like best. I shall let him have that answer following the completion of my estimates. Perhaps in about an hour's time I will be able to supply him with the answer.
There is no need to go into detail by way of a preliminary statement on these important estimates. My predecessor, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, on three previous occasions has had the privilege of guiding the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources through the House of Commons. I have reviewed the record of those debates and discussions and I am sure all members will agree that the pattern has been well established for the recent progress that has been made in all the multitudinous and multifarious activities of the department.
Then, too, I must mention the fact that unfortunately we are not able to have with us tonight the hon. member for Mackenzie River who has taken part in these discussions in a knowledgeable way during past years. As hon. members know, the hon. member for Mackenzie River has had a very serious illness extending over a long period of time, and I am sure we all regret his absence tonight and wish for him a speedy recovery. However, we do have another genuine northerner with us tonight, the hon. member for Yukon. He is the only hon. member able to be present tonight representing that great area of

Canada north of the 60th parallel which constitutes 40 per cent of Canada's land area and he will carry the main burden and responsibility for bringing all the pertinent problems before members of the committee.
I came to this portfolio less than six months ago and during the intervening time 1 have been busily engaged in making myself acquainted with the functions of the department in Ottawa as well as with the departmental officials and personnel here in Ottawa. I am very happy to inform members of the committee that during that time I have had the opportunity of meeting every member at work in the department here in Ottawa. That alone is a formidable task. I am not sure of the exact number of personnel in Ottawa but I understand it is approximately 700.
More recently I have visited the territory itself, having travelled in the Yukon during the Christmas recess and in the Northwest Territories during the Easter recess, and within two weeks I hope to be able to have a bird's-eye view of the important area of the north that we call the eastern Arctic or the Canadian archipelago. When I have completed this itinerary I will have had personal contact with the people in places that until recently were almost unknown in the southern part of Canada but which because of the upsurge in activity in recent years are rapidly becoming household words in the Canadian nation.
By way of introduction, I should like to make a brief reference to the administrative responsibility of the minister of this department. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources consists of an administration services branch and five operating branches. There are important interrelationships between these five operating branches. As members look through the blue book of estimates they may find some difficulty in finding any apparent interrelationship with respect to some of the branches that come under the general heading of northern affairs and national resources. It is true that there are some dissimilarities in the objectives, aims and activities of the national museum, for example, and those of the water resources branch or the national parks branch on the one hand and the northern administration branch on the other. Similarly, the Canadian government travel bureau would at first glance appear to bear little real relationship to other areas of the department's work. Yet it seems clear that activities designed to assist such an important resource-based industry as tourism have an appropriate place in the national resources department.
Having called attention to the great diversity in the work of these five interrelated branches, it seems to me it would make for 90205-6-244J
Supply-Northern Affairs more orderly discussion if I did not attempt in this opening statement to go into any detail with respect to the various branches. I shall therefore restrict myself to a few general observations on the department as a whole, particularly in relation to the votes shown under departmental administration, of which there are four. If it is the wish of the committee I will be glad to make statements on each of the five branches as the appropriate items are reached. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I am entirely in the hands of the committee in this respect. It might be that members of the committee in their general statements might touch on points that I would otherwise have considered, which I think will obviate the necessity of repetition on my part.
Hon. members will note that the department's estimates for the coming year total nearly $84 million compared with some $88 J million last year when the various supplementary items for 1960-61 are included. Comparisons between the two years, however, are somewhat misleading since last year's estimates included an amount of nearly $7-| million for the forestry branch which is now a part of the new Department of Forestry. It is evident, therefore, that instead of a decrease of S4million there is in fact an increase of about $3 million over the previous year when the forestry figures are excluded.
It seems to me that one of the most important developments of recent years in this department was the government's decision to give greater recognition to the importance of the forest-based industries in the Canadian economy by the creation of a separate fulltime ministry. This is in line, of course, with the emphasis on national development which was so clearly set before the committee on previous occasions by my predecessor in this office. I should like to pay tribute to Dr. Harrison, the deputy minister of forestry, and his colleagues for the excellent work they have done over the years as an important part of my department, and also to Dr. Prebble and his associates from the former forest biology division of the Department of Agriculture. So far as I am concerned, my contact with these gentlemen was in the form of a hail and farewell because they were already in the process of transition when I took over the portfolio. Already there is evidence that these men, under the leadership of my colleague, the Minister of Forestry, are creating from out of the two units an effective and smooth functioning organization which, in co-operation with the provinces, will more adequately fulfil the federal government's responsibilities in this very important field.

Supply-Northern Affairs
Looking ahead-I must make some reference to this event because of its importance-the most notable event for the department during the coming year will be the resources for tomorrow conference scheduled to take place in Montreal next October. The first item in the estimates, vote No. 279, includes an amount of $80,000, the details of which can be found on page 399 of the blue book, which is the federal share of the expenses for this conference. The provincial governments have agreed to contribute $40,000 which will bring the total budget for the conference to $120,000.
During the course of the session so far certain hon. members have maintained an interest in the plans for this conference as indicated by their questions from time to time on orders of the day. I hope that this interest will continue because I feel that if the success of the conference is going to be assured every hon. member will share some responsibility for publicizing it and making it as widely known in their respective constituencies as possible.
When I was first a member of this house, I can recall that year after year there was an annual call on private members' day for a conference of this kind. At last, the conference is going to become a reality. The hon. member for Port Arthur has been one of the persistent inquirers-I was going to say inquisitors, but I think inquirers is a better word-about this conference. I trust he will have something to say during the discussion of the estimates.
The other day a question was raised about the participants in the conference. I am happy to be able to inform the committee that there will be some 600 persons attending from governments, business, industries, universities and various interested organizations. The conference is long overdue. It is being called to ascertain what is being done across the nation with regard to the management of our renewable resources, the gaps which exist and what should be done in the future to assure wise management of these important resources. Water pollution will be a subject for discussion. Water was once regarded as boundless and plentiful in Canada. In some settled areas of our nation we have been confronted recently by a real problem of polluted waters. Legislation to deal with this matter has already been considered. I refer to the passage of legislation last fall providing assistance to municipalities for the construction of sewage disposal facilities. This is the sort of thing that anticipates what we feel will be the results of the conference.
Another piece of legislation which anticipates what we feel and what we hope will come out of the conference concerns the
IMr. Dinsdale.]
A.R.D.A. program which is a massive and comprehensive approach to the wise management of our soil and water resources. This bill is still before the house. No doubt there will be much useful and helpful discussion in respect of these important renewable resources. I shall leave the discussion of the resources for tomorrow's conference at that stage and just indicate that the plans are going forward. Perhaps if hon. members have any further questions we can consider them after those questions have been placed before the committee.
Research has been a topic of continuing discussion in Canada, particularly research in the north. Hon. members will notice that the second item in the estimates, vote No. 280, provides for the operation of the northern co-ordination and research centre, including a grant to the Arctic institute of North America and grants in aid for northern research. The act under which the department is established gives the minister of northern affairs the responsibility for coordinating federal government activities in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and also for fostering, through scientific investigation, knowledge of the Canadian north and of the means for dealing with conditions related to its further development.
The northern co-ordination and research centre sponsors and conducts research in those areas that are outside the sphere of responsibility of other departments. The increase of $19,780 in this vote is to provide for a modest expansion in the program and meet the increased cost of salaries.
The research program is going forward. There are some who will say that it is not going forward rapidly enough, but I do want to point out to hon. members that there has been a considerable expansion and increase in activity in this important area during recent years.
I think, Mr. Chairman, with these general references to the estimates by way of getting the discussion initiated tonight, I shall resume my place. I could have continued by talking about the progress of our roads to resources program which is covered by vote No. 282. Perhaps I should mention that this program now covers all ten Canadian provinces. In fact, my first formal duty when I became minister was the signing of the agreement with the province of Quebec which completed the national picture for participation in the roads to resources program. The expenditure to date under the roads to resources program is estimated at slightly more than $45 million, and federal payments already made to provinces exceed $20 million. When fully implemented, the program should produce some 4,500 miles of new and important

developmental roads in the provinces. At the moment 2,198 miles are under construction and 1,317 miles have been completed. We all recognize that in order to carry forward the program of national development that has been launched, it is necessary to provide access roads to our resources potential.
Before resuming my place I want to repeat that I shall be pleased to reply to general questions on departmental policy on the first vote or to questions of detail on any of these first four items. As I have indicated at the outset of my remarks, I shall be glad also to make short statements on each of the branches as the appropriate items are reached if that is the wish of the committee.

How can we discuss this department's estimates without referring to the great vision of 1958? We hear less and less about it now. It has become a mirage over the years. We remember the build-up and the high-pressure publicity that accompanied this vision of the north at election time in 1958. That vision was not based on facts, as I will prove in a few moments. And to prove this statement-I want to state an historic fact-I will refer to the 1955 estimates. I believe the present minister was then a member of the special committee, as I was also. So, I quote from a statement made by the former minister, now premier of the province of Quebec, when we were about to discuss the planning of northern affairs:
As I intimated the other day, we are firmly convinced that there are two fundamental problems in the Canadian north, problems that we have been actively considering since: first, the achievement of its economic development as an integral part of Canada; second, the adjustment of its native people to a new way of life. As I said last Wednesday we have to deal with two main problems; one is economic, the other is human.
In the economic field our policy is to develop the natural resources of the north to the maximum national advantage. The process will involve gainfully occupying more and more natives and attracting people to the north.
And on page 536:
As to water transportation we have had since January preliminary talks with the officers of the Northern Transportation Company, and we will have a further meeting with them next week. We are hopeful of obtaining a fair reduction in rates to and in the north. As to air transportation, the Canadian Pacific Air Lines has now before the air transport board an application for a reduction in their rates to and in the north. We have decided to have a more vigorous policy of road construction. We have already made provision for more road building.
The second problem is the human problem. This is the problem of the natives of the Northwest Territories. The nation as a whole gives them family allowances, old age pensions, and relief when indigent, but the broader need-and they are immediate needs-are health, education and a sound economy.
On page 539, he said:
The provision of more adequate primary education is most urgent in the Mackenzie valley ... All the hostels to be constructed within the next five years, except one, will be in the Mackenzie valley. The hostels will be constructed by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, which from the first of April this year-this week-will have responsibility for the education of Indians


as well as Eskimos in the Northwest Territories. The hostels will be turned over to either the Roman Catholic Church or the Anglican Church for operation (the Indians and Eskimos are almost entirely of one denomination or the other) according to location and the population to be served.
These proposals have been discussed fully with Bishop Marsh of the Church of England and Bishop Trocellier of the Roman Catholic Church. Both agree that it is the program best designed to meet the special needs of the north and to remove difficulties that have been increasing in recent years because of the inadequacy of school facilities in various localities for children of one faith or the other.
The above program will be implemented over a period of six years, with the first unit being started during the coming summer-1955.

Mr. Chairman, I have given an outline of our policy to cope with the human problem of economic development in the north. I do not believe our plans lack imagination, vigour or aggressiveness.

Mr. Chairman, a few days ago, the Secretary of State made a speech in Toronto. In that high-flown way of his, he was celebrating the virtues of the two great races which must unite and respect one another; the two great races be treated the same way. After such a lecture, I wonder if the minister would not consider changing his position. I think it is most urgent for his officers and for the minister to give those school children education in both languages, since the Eskimos are Canadian citizens and I think it cannot be tolerated that in one part of the country, particularly in northern Quebec, only the English language be taught in schools.
I urge the minister to look into that matter, to take the necessary steps in order to secure the services of bilingual people so that the young may receive their education in both languages. I urge him also to see to it-since that comes under his jurisdiction-that no books or manuals carry any detailed information that is not according to the historical truth. Of course, we have no Canadian flag and I fail to see why we should give these young people the false impression that the union jack is the symbol of Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have several other questions to put to the minister. I shall put them as we go on with his estimates. But I hope that he will bring us up to date on a matter which I feel is of capital and vital importance, that is northern development. Mr. Chairman, I would have been prepared to allow the hon. member to carry on but I wished to take the opportunity afforded me to say in all frankness to the minister that my colleagues and I are somewhat disappointed in his department, in that the former minister left it and went to the Department of Agriculture. I had hoped, with all respect to the present minister and his wonderful qualities, that we would have been given a new minister in this department with a tremendous amount of drive and flair. The present minister has been in this portfolio for several months so that we can make some judgment now, although certainly an incomplete one, as to whether he has revealed these qualities. This is a point not worth belabouring, but I can say we are still disappointed.
This department has been bisected, to a degree, in that we have the new Department of Forestry. As a result there have been considerable changes, and I am sure an administrative shakedown. I would like to point out to the minister that this department has probably had a more thorough investigation by a parliamentary committee than any other department of the government. The committee on mines, forests and waters, under the direction of the hon. member for Lambton

West, has examined the operations of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in some cases twice and thrice over. I do not think anyone looking at the reports of that committee, including last year's report specifically in regard to the water resources branch, could come to any optimistic conclusion as to the state of this department when this government took over. The conclusion I have come to, as a member of that committee for several years, is that the administration of that department is not the finest in the world. One has only to look at the recommendations made by the committee on mines, forests and waters during the past three years to recognize that the members of that committee felt that the administration of this department was falling behind. This applies to almost any aspect of that department. We are disappointed because this department has not had an extremely aggressive minister at the head of it.
I do not wish to press this point further, but one would hope that the minister at the head of the department, as well as the senior civil servants, were possessed of enough drive and imagination to implement some of the many recommendations presented to it by the parliamentary committee. We will be watching very closely to see whether the present minister is able to do this.
The previous minister initiated the gigantic resources for tomorrow conference which is to be held in Montreal in October of this year.
I would ask all hon. members to look at information bulletin No. 1 which we received not long ago. I am sure they will realize then the tremendous scope of this conference, both in breadth and depth, in terms of background papers and material. I feel this will be the greatest conference of its kind ever held in Canada.
Business of the House
In the criticisms I have made previously, relating to this conference, I pointed out to the previous minister that a similar conference took place during and after the first world war. The background papers and material produced at that time were quite extensive. I have had the opportunity of studying this material while a librarian in a forestry library, and I point out the similarity between some of those original papers and the papers regarding this proposed conference. I would also mention the similarity between the proposed topics of conversation for the conference this fall, and those topics of conversation at the conference during and after world war I. This similarity indicates a lack of progress in the renewable resources field.
